Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
When the car bomb detonated at the central transit hub, Kiet was arranging crates of medical supplies near the eastern checkpoint. He remembers the flash first, a stark white image burning behind his eyes, followed by the heavy glass of the departure boards shattering into a thousand dark fragments. Even now, he looks at the faded photograph of the damaged terminal and feels the scale of it drift just outside his reach, as though the story is too extreme to have happened to him. He knows the dates and the reports, yet the memory sits apart from his daily life. In the quiet of his kitchen, the auditory echoes return without warning: the sharp crack of the blast, the distant wail of a triage siren, the sudden gasp of a stranger beside him. These sounds surface unbidden, pulling his attention forward before he can check where he is or what he is doing. Kiet had come to believe that the world remained inherently volatile, and he stopped treating any open space as fully secure. Within weeks, his sense of safety contracted into a narrow circle: his home, the ground-floor office of the aid organization, and the perimeter of the community center. He found himself standing just inside doorways, shoulders squared, eyes tracking the perimeter of the room. Ordinary noises drew his gaze instantly; the hiss of the pressure cooker, the rhythmic thump of a neighbor’s lawnmower, even the soft click of his wife’s ceramic mug set on the counter, made him jump or startle at sounds that would not bother most people. His alertness settled into his posture, a constant watchfulness that kept his muscles tense and his breathing shallow, even when no new threat emerged. His mind turned over the event again and again. He repeatedly blamed himself for what happened, tracing his decisions back to that morning: if he had moved the supplies earlier, if he had stepped away from the glass, if he had signaled the guard to clear the line sooner. The self-reproach did not fade; it accumulated like sediment, settling into his routine. Alongside this internal questioning, his habits shifted. He began to avoid driving, finding that sitting in the passenger seat of any vehicle left him braced for impact, hands gripping his knees until he reached familiar ground. When he could not leave the house, he stayed in place. He also found himself sidestepping disagreement. When colleagues at the aid office debated logistics or funding priorities, Kiet would listen quietly, nod, and let the conversation pass, avoiding conflict; any rise in voices simply felt like a prelude to the kind of sudden disruption he had learned to expect. These changes were not abstract; they reshaped his days as a refugee aid worker. His work required constant coordination, yet his daily environment became a series of careful calculations. He avoided driving to satellite clinics, opting instead to walk the three blocks from his home, or he rode in the back of a colleague’s sedan, watching the road through tinted glass. The occupational consequence was tangible: he deferred to younger staff on field assignments, staying behind to manage paperwork in the office where the walls felt solid and the acoustics were predictable. His wife noticed how he would pause before opening the door to the street, how he would adjust his chair to face the entrance, how he would quietly yield his opinion during family dinners when the conversation grew loud or fast-paced. Now at seventy-two, Kiet sits in the therapist’s office with his hands folded over his cane, listening to the hum of the fluorescent lights and the occasional murmur of the waiting room. A quiet breaking point finally brought him through the door: a routine phone call about a supply shipment produced a sharp startle, and when his wife gently suggested they review his sleep and daytime alertness together, he realized he had been carrying the same weight for longer than he had admitted. His PCL-5 score of 53 mirrors the steady accumulation of these habits. He is not certain what will change, but he is hoping for a way to sit in a car without bracing for the worst, and to hear ordinary sounds without the old fear tightening his chest. He walks in now, still watchful, still replaying the image of the shattered glass, but ready to learn how to stay.
